title: How a Fake Delivery Text Nearly Cost Me My Savings
script: Narrator: [candid] I've always considered myself reasonably sharp about scams, which made what happened last month all the more humbling to admit out loud.
Narrator: [recalling] A text arrived claiming my package couldn't be delivered because of an unpaid customs fee, a small amount, barely worth questioning at a glance.
Narrator: [honest] What I didn't notice, distracted as I was between meetings, was that the link led to a domain that merely resembled the courier's actual website.
Narrator: [tense] I typed in my card details without a second thought, the way you'd sign a delivery slip without reading it, because the whole process felt utterly routine.
Narrator: [uneasy] It wasn't until an hour later, scrolling absentmindedly, that something nagged at me: I hadn't actually ordered anything requiring international shipping that week.
Narrator: [urgent] I checked my bank app immediately, and there it was, a transaction I hadn't authorized, already pending, for considerably more than the fee I'd supposedly paid.
Narrator: [relieved] Thankfully, my bank flagged the second, larger charge as suspicious and froze it before it cleared, which spared me a genuinely painful conversation with myself.
Narrator: [reflective] Looking back, every warning sign had been sitting there in plain view: the mismatched link, the vague wording, the urgency designed to override careful thinking.
Narrator: [wry] Scammers, it turns out, are far less interested in fooling your intelligence than in exploiting the thirty seconds when you're too rushed to use it.
Narrator: [determined] Since then, I've made a rule for myself: any message demanding immediate payment gets closed, and I contact the company directly through channels I already trust.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I've also started warning my parents, who I suspect are targeted more often precisely because they're less inclined to question anything official-looking.
Narrator: [warm] My mother laughed when I explained it, then admitted she'd nearly clicked something similar herself the week before, which sobered us both considerably.
Narrator: [with a small smile] These days, whenever an urgent text arrives claiming disaster is imminent unless I act within minutes, I treat that urgency itself as the clearest red flag of all.
